description: Grade 12 student from J. Clarke Richardson Collegiate.
summary:
Eye of the Storm is a browser game where the player designs a satellite mission to track hurricanes and warn coastal cities in time.

The player works through the phases of a real mission. They read the mission brief, then run a trade study: choosing an orbit, science instruments, solar panels, an antenna, ground stations and a rocket. Every choice costs mass, power, money or data, and a live dashboard and a team of advisors show the effects straight away. After a launch readiness review, the satellite flies a full storm season. The player makes decisions along the way, such as how to respond to a solar flare or a failing instrument, and the design's spare margins decide how those turn out. A mission report then explains why the mission succeeded or failed and which real NASA mission the design resembles.

There is no single right answer: three different orbits can all succeed. The game shows that mission design is about trade-offs, and why margins matter.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Eye of the Storm is a single-player browser game about designing a satellite mission to track hurricanes. The player is given a mission brief and a fixed budget, then works through a real mission's phases:

1. Trade study. Choose an orbit (low Earth orbit, a three-satellite constellation, or geostationary orbit), science instruments, solar panels, an antenna, ground stations and a rocket. A live dashboard shows budget, mass, power and data, plus a forecast score with the pass mark. Team advisors point out weak spots.

2. Launch readiness review. The design cannot launch if it is over budget, too heavy for the rocket, or missing a part.

3. Operations. The satellite flies a 120-day storm season. Each storm is scored at landfall on how good the forecast was. The season pauses several times for a decision, such as a solar flare, a failing instrument or a ground station outage.

4. Mission report. The game gives a score out of 100, explains what helped and what hurt, and names the real mission the design most resembles (GOES-R, TROPICS, CYGNSS, GPM or Suomi NPP/JPSS).

HOW IT WORKS

Every part has a mass, power use, cost and data rate. The game combines them into two measures: watch time (how often the satellite sees a storm) and detail (how much the instruments reveal). The forecast score needs both. Geostationary orbit watches constantly but from far away. Low Earth orbit sees sharp detail but passes only occasionally. A constellation sits in between and costs more. The outcome of each mid-mission decision depends on the spare power, data and mass the player left in the design.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game teaches that mission design is a set of trade-offs with no single right answer: all three orbits can succeed. Players learn why engineers keep margins, because a design with no spare capacity suffers when something goes wrong. Linking each design to a real mission gives players a starting point to learn more about NASA's Earth-observing fleet. It is aimed at students and beginners, and a short tutorial explains the screen on first play.

TOOLS

Python with the pygame-ce library, built for the browser with pygbag and hosted on itch.io. Sound effects and the hurricane graphics are generated in code. AI for some coding and testing.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz or a sandbox, the game gives the player one concrete job: warn coastal cities in time. The same design choices matter twice, first on the dashboard and again during the storm season when the decisions test the margins. Easy and Hard modes change the budget and the number of storms.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Accuracy against playability: costs and masses are simplified and are not real mission data, but the trade-offs follow how real missions behave.

- Fairness: thousands of simulated seasons were used to check that the dashboard predicts the result, that luck has a small effect, and that all three orbits can win.

- Accessibility: it runs in a browser with only a mouse, and the sound can be muted with the M key.
